title: How Existential Risks Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss existential risks: threats that could wipe out humanity or permanently cripple its potential. They open with a note that the episode was recorded before the COVID-19 pandemic and released during it. They cover why existential risks differ from ordinary catastrophes (no second chance; time and proximity as survival factors), the history of the field (nuclear war, John Leslie, Nick Bostrom, Carl Sagan's "technological adolescence"), Bostrom's categories (extinction, permanent stagnation, flawed realization), natural risks (asteroids, supervolcanoes, gamma-ray bursts) versus human-made risks (AI misalignment, nanotechnology and the gray goo hypothesis, engineered pathogens, collider experiments and vacuum decay), climate change as probably not an existential risk, and why the future matters. They recommend Toby Ord's book The Precipice and the Future of Humanity Institute and Future of Life Institute, and close with listener mail about Weird Science and the phrase "wolf bait."

segments.summary: Josh explains the episode was recorded before COVID-19 and released during the pandemic, framing existential risk thinking as relevant to looking out for each other. Hosts banter about Tommy Chong, Dave, and Josh's earlier series The End of the World.
topics: The End of the World with Josh Clark

segments.title: Defining existential risk
segments.summary: Existential risks are threats that could wipe out all of humanity, with no second chance. Unlike ordinary disasters, survival has depended on time and proximity, and mudslides and local catastrophes do not qualify. A near-total loss that leaves survivors who could rebuild would not necessarily be existential.

segments.title: History of the field and nuclear war
segments.summary: The hosts trace the field's origins. Nuclear war was early focus, with Russell and Einstein's manifesto and Carl Sagan's work. John Leslie in the nineties broadened the scope to technological threats, and Nick Bostrom became a founder. Nuclear war is probably survivable and recoverable over a long timescale.

segments.title: Caring about future generations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why people care about distant future people, and how Toby Ord argues that caring about people on the other side of the world extends to people in future times. They discuss self-interest, ego, and how upbringing shapes responsibility.

segments.title: Bostrom's types: extinction, stagnation, flawed realization
segments.summary: Extinction is the most obvious existential risk. Permanent stagnation means civilization can never recover its progress, illustrated by a climate geoengineering disaster. Flawed realization means a permanent dictatorship or technology-enabled control, like the Matrix, that prevents humanity from fulfilling its potential.

segments.title: Natural versus human-made risks
segments.summary: Natural risks include asteroids, comets, gamma-ray bursts, and supervolcanic eruptions. They are rare and hard to act on. Human-made risks are more concerning because humans can control and mitigate them, though that also makes them ironic.

segments.title: AI, nanotechnology, and engineered pathogens
segments.summary: Artificial intelligence is considered the most worrying risk, because safe, aligned AI is harder than expected while unsafe AI is profitable; the paperclip thought experiment illustrates misaligned goals. Nanotechnology raises the gray goo scenario, which Eric Drexler later backed away from. Biotechnology accidents and engineered pathogens with lab leak potential are also discussed.

segments.title: Particle collider and vacuum decay risks
segments.summary: Physics experiments such as the Large Hadron Collider might theoretically create microscopic black holes or a low-energy vacuum bubble that could expand and destroy the universe. Hosts note this is not in Toby Ord's book and that it is speculative. Climate change is discussed as serious but probably not an existential risk, though worst cases could be worse than expected.

segments.title: Technological adolescence and the importance of the future
segments.summary: Carl Sagan's technological adolescence describes the dangerous period before technological maturity. Only one catastrophe is needed. Toby Ord estimates about a one in six chance over the next century. The rope analogy by J. L. Schellenberg shows humanity's potential lifespan far exceeds what has passed. The hosts argue for a multi-pronged, global effort, and mention learning to live off Earth as a hedge.

segments.title: Closing and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts recommend The Precipice, the End of the World series, and the Future of Humanity and Future of Life institutes. Listener Jake's email about the phrase wolf bait in Weird Science closes the episode.
